You might have trouble getting the wi-fi or ethernet card to work. They may require non-free, proprietary drivers to function. Installing such drivers encroaches your freedom. They are available, though.

The biggest issue you are going to run into is drivers. A lot of laptop manufactures use their own versions of chipsets. So things like WiFi, ethernet, soundcards, touchscreen, trackpads, etc may not work right from a fresh default install. You are going to have to do your research, you'll have to see what chipset drivers are included in whichever distribution of Linux you want versus what chipsets are used in the laptop. Then whichever ones aren't included already, you'll have to see if a Linux driver exists and you can load it in after.

Generally, the older the chipset, the greater chance it has made it into the Linux kernel. But keep in mind, not all Linux Distributions are using the latest kernels either.

The next issue is secure boot. Some newer laptops have no known way to turn off secure boot, which generally means you aren't going to be able to load any OS onto it besides what comes with it pre-installed, aka MS Windows 10. Secure boot is bad.

What you're describing sounds more like the Linux command line than Linux in general. It's a large set of powerful commands that can pass results on to one another. You can issue simple commands or write programs in the command line's various languages to do more complicated things. Not all of Linux runs in that environment though. The heavy work is done by some main background processes. These processes generally take care of a whole area of related work by themselves. If they need to communicate with the kernel or other processes, they usually do it by faster means than passing strings to one another like the command like tools do.

systemd doesn't have much to do with the Linux command line. It was proposed as a way to standardize and improve the system that starts and controls the system's main background processes.
